title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an analytical AI platform can support lesson-planning feedback in teacher education and whether such support performs as well as or better than human feedback. The authors focus on a practical problem in university-based teacher preparation: instructors often cannot provide frequent, detailed, individualized feedback on lengthy lesson plans, especially when student numbers are large. They also note concerns often associated with AI in education, including transparency, bias, reproducibility, and data protection, and position their system as an alternative to generative AI by using analytical rather than text-generating methods.

The intervention is EDDA, an analytical AI platform that classifies uploaded lesson plans and materials using a BERT-based model and returns expert-level feedback across 10 main categories and 57 subcategories. In the study, one group of master’s-level vocational business education students received AI feedback during a semester and could then discuss the output with a university teacher; a control group received human feedback only. The study was longitudinal, with lesson plans collected at the beginning and end of the semester, and with repeated survey measures of AI literacy, AI attitudes, digital competences, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and motivation.

The sample consisted of 103 students in master’s programs for business education in Germany, working in small groups. The study found that AI feedback can match or surpass human feedback on some lesson-planning dimensions, especially several sustainability-related and pedagogical criteria such as social competences, reflexivity, action orientation, lesson structure, learner engagement, and some technology-related aspects. However, the authors also found that simply using AI did not automatically improve AI literacy, motivation, or attitudes, and they emphasize that the platform works best as part of a holistic, teacher-supported framework. They additionally report that some categories in the training data were weaker, which could lead the system to underestimate planning quality and potentially discourage users.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / large language model-based chatbot or AI feedback system with no specific commercial product named.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses generative AI generally as a comparator and as a source of potential risks for feedback, but the empirical intervention used EDDA, an analytical AI platform rather than a generative chatbot.

identified_tools.name: Adaptive Feedback System (General)
identified_tools.description: A general analytical AI feedback platform that classifies uploaded lesson plans against predefined criteria and returns individualized expert feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper’s empirical intervention was EDDA (electronic didactic assistance for lesson planning), an analytical AI platform used throughout a longitudinal semester intervention to provide feedback on lesson plans in vocational teacher education.

findings.finding_summary: In a longitudinal intervention with N=103 vocational business education master’s students, EDDA feedback improved some lesson-plan dimensions relative to human feedback, including sustainability-related planning aspects. The paper reports significant positive effects for SDG 15 (life on land; p<0.10), social competences for sustainable development (p<0.05), and reflexivity (p<0.10), while other sustainability dimensions showed no significant intervention effect.
findings.measure: Content analysis ratings of lesson plans for SDGs and competences for sustainable change agents

findings.finding_summary: The study reports that EDDA can supplement traditional feedback because it provides reproducible, individualized expert feedback on lesson plans, but it also tends to underestimate planning performance. The authors explicitly note that this could potentially have demotivating effects because it may mask competence development, and they identify low reliability in some categories as a limitation that increases the potential for error in recommendations.
findings.measure: Expert feedback quality / reliability of automated lesson-plan feedback

findings.finding_summary: For the meta-dimensions, the mere use of the AI platform did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes, or motivation. The abstract states that results show the mere use of AI does not automatically enhance AI literacy, change attitudes, or improve motivation; the control and experimental groups did not show clear intervention-driven gains on these broad measures over the semester.
findings.measure: Self-reported AI literacy, AI attitudes, motivation, self-efficacy with digital technologies, and digital competences

quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal intervention study with a comparison group and repeated use across a semester, which is stronger than a simple cross-sectional design. However, it is not randomized in the traditional sense and the sample is relatively small, with some measures and categories showing reliability limitations.
impact_tier_rationale: The intervention shows modest positive effects on some lesson-plan dimensions, but the paper also reports null effects for broader AI literacy, attitudes, and motivation, plus a potential negative downside from underestimation that could demotivate users. Overall impact appears mixed and generally modest rather than large.
